mainTopic: Examining blood: which sages ruled on it and why, the limits on overturning another חכם's ruling, trusting a woman's report, and judging color by what is seen in proper light
overview: This amud is about the skill and caution needed to examine blood (ראיית דמים). It opens by saying only the wise רבי חנינא could examine blood his special way. Then several sages explain why they did or did not examine blood: רבי יוחנן, רבי זירא, עולא and רב יהודה each held back for their own reasons, while רבי אלעזר took it on, learning from רבי חנינא's humility. Stories about רבי אלעזר and רבא, who recognized דם חימוד by smell and passed a test of sixty kinds of blood, show how great real expertise was. The story of ילתא, whose blood one sage ruled impure and another pure, raises the rule that one חכם may not overturn another's strict ruling. It also raises the question of whether a woman is believed about blood and about a חכם's ruling. Both proofs for that last question are pushed away, and it stays unresolved on this amud. The גמרא then explains רבי's three changing rulings on one stain: a judge goes only by what his eyes see. It ends with the right lighting for checking blood and returns to the משנה's color of diluted wine, with a ברייתא that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Only רבי חנינא was wise enough to examine this way
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא's method of examining blood is limited to him alone, because he was unusually wise.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was רבי חנינא who was wise enough for this. Everyone else is not that wise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits the method of examining blood that it just described for רבי חנינא. It says only he could use it, because ordinary people are not that skilled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The method itself is not rejected. It is just not a general rule for everyone. It depended on רבי חנינא's personal skill, and this sets up the next statements about רבי חנינא's greatness.

phrases.english: It is Rabbi Chanina who is wise,
everyone else is not so wise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the earlier report of רבי חנינא's examination method to him alone.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי חנינא's method of examining blood was only for him. Others are not skilled enough to copy it.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן stopped examining blood because of רבי חנינא's wisdom
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that he stopped ruling on blood because רבי חנינא kept reaching the opposite result.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: רבי חנינא's wisdom made me stop examining blood. When I said impure, he said pure. When I said pure, he said impure.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן tells us why he personally does not examine blood. Every time he ruled, רבי חנינא ruled the opposite way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Seeing a greater expert always reach the opposite answer showed רבי יוחנן that he could not trust his own judgment about blood. So he pulled back from ruling on blood altogether.

keyTerms.meaning: examine blood (to rule טמא or טהור)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
The wisdom of Rabbi Chanina
caused me not to examine blood,
when I would declare it impure, he would declare it pure,
when I would declare it pure, he would declare it impure.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: חֻכְמְתָא דְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא גְּרַמָא לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the praise of רבי חנינא's wisdom by showing how it affected רבי יוחנן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because רבי חנינא always disagreed with his rulings, רבי יוחנן stopped examining blood.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר began examining blood because of רבי חנינא's humility
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר reasons the opposite way. If the humble רבי חנינא was willing to take on the risk of examining blood, so should he.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: רבי חנינא's humility made me examine blood. If רבי חנינא, who is humble, puts himself into a situation of doubt and examines, should I not examine?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר gives the opposite personal reaction to רבי יוחנן. רבי חנינא's example pushed him to start examining blood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר focuses on רבי חנינא's humility, not his wisdom. A humble person might hold back from deciding hard questions. But רבי חנינא still accepted the risk of ruling, so a less humble person has no excuse to refuse. The argument uses the pattern 'ומה... אני לא?'

keyTerms.meaning: puts himself into a situation of doubt and risk
'if even...': opens a 'how much more so' argument

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
The humility of Rabbi Chanina
caused me to examine blood,
for if Rabbi Chanina, who is humble,
puts himself into doubt and examines,
phrases.notes: The "doubt" is the risk of ruling wrongly on a hard question.

phrases.english: should I not examine?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: עִנְוְותָנוּתָא דְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא גְּרַמָא לִי דַּחֲזַאי דְּמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite reaction to רבי יוחנן's. The same רבי חנינא led רבי אלעזר to examine rather than refrain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אלעזר examined blood, learning from the humble רבי חנינא who was willing to rule despite the risk.

steps.title: רבי זירא refrained because he did not understand the nature of בבל
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא did not examine blood. He reasoned that if he did not understand the nature of the people of בבל, he surely could not understand blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: the nature of בבל made me not examine blood. I said to myself: I don't understand that nature, so how can I claim to understand blood?
steps.whatsHappening: A third אמורא gives his personal reason for not examining blood. His reason is his lack of understanding of the people of בבל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא argues from the easier to the harder. If he could not grasp something simpler, he certainly could not grasp something as hard as telling types of blood apart. This sets up the גמרא's next question about how these two things are connected.

keyTerms.meaning: nature, character (here, of the people of בבל)

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
The nature of Babylonia caused me
not to examine blood,
for I said: about nature I don't know,
so about blood I would know?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא: טִבְעָא דְּבָבֶל גְּרַמָא לִי דְּלָא חֲזַאי דְּמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third personal approach, which agrees with רבי יוחנן's choice not to examine but for a different reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי זירא did not examine blood, because he did not understand the nature of the people of בבל.

steps.title: Does blood depend on understanding nature? רבה knew one but not the other
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי זירא's link between the two kinds of knowledge. רבה understood the nature of בבל, yet he still did not know blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean the matter depends on knowing nature? But רבה knew about nature, and he did not know about blood!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions רבי זירא's reasoning. It points to רבה as a person who had the first kind of knowledge but still lacked the second.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא seemed to assume that knowing nature leads to knowing blood. רבה's case shows that this is not true. Knowing nature did not give him the ability to judge blood, so the link looks broken.

keyTerms.meaning: is this to say...? (opens a challenge to an implied idea)

phrases.english: Is this to say that the matter depends on nature?
But Rabba is one who knew about nature,
and he did not know about blood!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the logic behind רבי זירא's statement.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי זירא's apparent assumption that knowing nature is what gives a person the knowledge of blood.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Counter-example: רבה had the knowledge of nature but still lacked knowledge of blood, so the one does not depend on the other.

steps.title: רבי זירא meant an all-the-more-so argument based on רבה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רבי זירא was making a כל שכן argument. If even רבה, who understood nature, did not examine blood, all the more so should he not.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was saying a 'how much more so': if רבה, who knew about nature, did not examine blood, should I examine?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reading רבי זירא's words differently. He was not claiming that blood depends on nature. He was using רבה as his model.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge from רבה actually becomes רבי זירא's own argument. רבה was above him in knowledge, since he understood nature, and still held back from examining blood. So רבי זירא, who did not even have that knowledge, should certainly hold back.

keyTerms.meaning: all the more so (an argument from a stronger case)

steps.whatToRemember: Three reactions to רבי חנינא and to the difficulty of blood: רבי יוחנן refrained because of his wisdom, רבי אלעזר examined because of his humility, and רבי זירא refrained with a כל שכן based on רבה.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי זירא claimed that understanding nature gives you the skill to judge blood. He was only comparing himself to רבה, a greater person who still held back.

phrases.english: He was saying an all-the-more-so:
if Rabba, who knew about nature,
did not examine blood, should I examine?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the קשיא by turning רבה's example into the basis of רבי זירא's reasoning.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the statement's logic: a כל שכן argument, not a claim that one kind of knowledge causes the other.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי זירא meant that knowing nature is what lets a person judge blood.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי זירא meant that if the greater רבה, who knew nature, still did not examine blood, then all the more so he should not.

steps.title: עולא refuses to examine blood in פומבדיתא
steps.stepSummary: עולא visits פומבדיתא and will not examine blood. He reasons that if the great רבי אלעזר did not examine blood when visiting רבי יהודה's place, he should not either.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא came to פומבדיתא. People brought him blood to examine, but he would not look at it. He said: If רבי אלעזר, the master of ארץ ישראל, would not examine blood when he came to רבי יהודה's place, should I examine it?!
steps.whatsHappening: Another sage, עולא, joins the list of sages who held back from examining blood. He gives his own reason, based on the example of רבי אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of 'if even he, then surely I' reasoning we saw with רבי זירא in step 6. If even a sage as great as רבי אלעזר held back when he was in another sage's town, then עולא, who sees himself as lesser, should surely hold back in פומבדיתא too.

keyTerms.meaning: he did not look at (examine) it
master of the land of Israel, a title for its greatest scholar

phrases.english: Ulla happened to come to Pumbedita,
they brought blood before him, and he would not look at it.
He said: Now if Rabbi Elazar,
who was the master of the land of Israel,
when he would come to the place of Rabbi Yehuda
would not examine blood,
shall I examine it?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another sage who did not examine blood, using the same 'if even he, surely I' reasoning as step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עולא would not examine blood in פומבדיתא, because even רבי אלעזר did not do so in רבי יהודה's place.

steps.title: Why was רבי אלעזר called master of the land of Israel
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רבי אלעזר got the title 'master of ארץ ישראל'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why did they call him 'master of the land of Israel'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses on the title עולא used for רבי אלעזר and asks what earned him that name. This sets up a story in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא's argument only works if רבי אלעזר really was an outstanding expert. So the גמרא asks for the basis of his title, and the answer will show his skill in examining blood specifically.

phrases.english: And why did they call him
"master of the land of Israel"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the title עולא gave רבי אלעזר in step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What event earned רבי אלעזר the title 'master of ארץ ישראל'?

steps.title: רבי אלעזר identifies blood of desire
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר smelled a woman's blood and said it came from desire, not from her period. רבי אמי checked with her and found he was right, and praised him with a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain woman brought blood before רבי אלעזר, while רבי אמי sat before him. רבי אלעזר smelled it and told her: This is blood of desire. After she left, רבי אמי went after her to ask. She told him: My husband was away traveling, and I longed for him. רבי אמי applied this verse to רבי אלעזר: 'The secret of ה׳ is with those who fear Him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a story. רבי אלעזר identified the cause of a woman's bleeding just by smelling it, and she confirmed he was right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דם חימוד is bleeding caused by longing, not menstrual blood. רבי אלעזר figured this out with no information about her life. רבי אמי checked and saw it was true, so he called it Heaven-given wisdom. That is why רבי אלעזר earned his great title.

keyTerms.meaning: blood of desire, bleeding caused by longing, not menstrual blood
went after her, looked into her case
ה׳'s secret is with those who fear Him

phrases.english: For a certain woman who brought
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some have the word in square brackets. Both mean 'who brought'.

phrases.english: blood before Rabbi Elazar,
and Rabbi Ami was sitting before him.
He smelled it, and said to her:
This is blood of desire.

phrases.aramaic: בָּתַר דְּנָפְקָה, אִטְּפַל לַהּ רַבִּי אַמֵּי.
phrases.english: After she left, Rabbi Ami went after her to look into it.
She said to him: My husband was away on the road
and I longed for him.
He read about him: "The secret of ה׳ is with those who fear Him."

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּהַהִיא אִתְּתָא דְּאַיְיתַאי דְּמָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8's question with a story.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אלעזר identified דם חימוד by smell alone, and the woman confirmed it. This showed his Heaven-given wisdom.

steps.title: רבא identifies the queen mother's blood, and her son doubts him
steps.stepSummary: איפרא הורמיז, the mother of King שבור, sent blood to רבא. He said it was blood of desire. She praised the wisdom of the Jews, but her son said it might have been a lucky guess.
steps.simpleTranslation: איפרא הורמיז, mother of King שבור, sent blood to רבא. רב עובדיה was sitting before him and saw רבא smell it. רבא told her: This is blood of desire. She said to her son: Come see how wise the Jews are! He told her: Maybe it was like a blind man finding the window, just a lucky hit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story of a sage reading blood by smell, this time רבא. The son's doubt sets up a test in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא matches רבי אלעזר's skill by spotting דם חימוד. But the king's doubt raises a fair point: one correct answer could be luck. This leads straight into the test that will prove it was not.

keyTerms.meaning: the wise ones of the Jews
like a blind man at an opening; a lucky hit

phrases.english: Ifra Hormiz, the mother of King Shapur,
sent blood before Rava.

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה יָתֵיב רַב עוֹבַדְיָה קַמֵּיהּ, אַרְחֵיהּ.
phrases.english: Rav Ovadya was sitting before him, and he smelled it.
phrases.notes: The one who smelled it is רבא. רב עובדיה is the one who saw it happen.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לַהּ: הַאי דַּם חִימּוּד הוּא.
phrases.english: He said to her: This is blood of desire.
She said to her son:
Come see how wise the Jews are!
He said to her: Maybe it was like a blind man at the opening.
phrases.notes: Picture a blind man who just stumbles onto the opening. It was a lucky guess.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִפְרָא הוֹרְמִיז, אִמֵּיהּ דְּשַׁבּוּר מַלְכָּא, שַׁדַּרָה דְּמָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel story to step 9, showing another sage's skill with דם חימוד, now followed by a challenge from the king.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא identified the queen-mother's blood as דם חימוד. Her son suggested it might have been luck.

steps.title: רבא passes the test of sixty kinds of blood
steps.stepSummary: The queen mother sent sixty kinds of blood, and רבא identified all of them. The last one was lice blood, which he did not know, but with Heaven's help he sent her a lice comb. She declared that the Jews can see into people's hearts.
steps.simpleTranslation: She then sent him sixty kinds of blood, and he identified all of them. The last one was lice blood, and he did not know it. But Heaven helped him: he sent her a comb that kills lice. She said: Jews, you dwell in the chambers of the heart!
steps.whatsHappening: The queen tests רבא with sixty samples to answer her son's doubt. רבא's success, plus help from Heaven on the last one, proves his skill was real.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One correct answer could be luck, but sixty cannot. Even where רבא's own knowledge ran out, Heaven helped him, which echoes 'סוד ה׳ ליראיו' from step 9. The story ends with even an outsider declaring the Jews' wisdom.

keyTerms.meaning: in the inner chambers of the heart

steps.whatToRemember: Some sages held back from examining blood, each for his own reason: רבי יוחנן, רבי זירא and עולא. Those who did examine it, like רבי אלעזר and רבא, showed amazing skill that was described as help from Heaven.

phrases.aramaic: הֲדַר שַׁדַּרָה לֵיהּ שִׁתִּין מִינֵי דְּמָא,
phrases.english: She then sent him sixty kinds of blood,
and he identified all of them.

phrases.aramaic: הַהוּא בָּתְרָא דָּם כִּנִּים הֲוָה, וְלָא יְדַע.
phrases.english: That last one was blood of lice, and he did not know it.
The matter was helped along,
phrases.notes: He got help from Heaven without realizing it.

phrases.english: and he sent her a comb that kills lice.
She said: Jews, you dwell in the chambers of the heart!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲדַר שַׁדַּרָה לֵיהּ שִׁתִּין מִינֵי דְּמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the son's doubt from step 10 by showing רבא succeeded with all sixty samples.
steps.raayaObject: That רבא's identification of the blood was real expertise, not a lucky guess.
steps.raayaSupportSource: He correctly identified all sixty samples, and Heaven helped him with the last one.

steps.title: Why רב יהודה stopped examining blood
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה used to examine blood, but stopped once his wife told him that the first drop is never brought to the sages because it is not clean.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: At first I used to examine blood. But once my wife, the mother of my son יצחק, told me, 'We don't bring this first drop to the sages, because it is not clean,' I stopped examining blood.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה tells us he used to rule on blood stains but stopped. The reason is something his wife told him about how women actually bring blood to the sages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first drop is not shown to the sages because other things are mixed into it. That means the sage only ever sees later drops, while the first drop, which might be impure, is never checked. So רב יהודה felt he could not rule properly and stopped examining.

keyTerms.meaning: I would 'see' blood, meaning examine it to rule pure or impure
Not clean, mixed with other things

steps.confusionAlert: 'Seeing blood' here does not mean just looking at it. It means examining blood to give a halachic ruling on whether the woman is pure or impure.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
At first I would examine blood,
but once she said to me,
the mother of my son Yitzchak,
'This first drop'
we do not bring it before the Rabbis,
because it is not clean,'
I no longer examine.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה מֵרֵישָׁא הֲוָה חָזֵינָא דְּמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of stories about sages examining blood, now with a sage who stopped doing it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יהודה stopped examining blood because the first drop, which might be impure, is never shown to the sages.

steps.title: The one kind of case רב יהודה still examines
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה adds that when the question is whether a woman is טמאה or טהורה, he certainly still examines.
steps.simpleTranslation: But to decide between impure and pure, I certainly examine.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה limits what he just said. There is one kind of question he still rules on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His worry was that the first drop, which might be impure, never reaches the חכם. Here the woman has been bleeding for a long time, so the blood he sees is clean and nothing is hidden from him, and he still examines it. This is an exception to his general practice, not a change in it.

phrases.english: Between impure and pure —
phrases.notes: This seems to mean a woman after childbirth whose days of purity are over. Her blood has been flowing a long time, so it is clean.

phrases.english: I certainly examine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רב יהודה's statement in step 12 by naming a case he still examines.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: To decide between טמאה and טהורה, רב יהודה still examines the blood.

steps.title: ילתא takes her blood to two different sages
steps.stepSummary: ילתא brought blood to רבה בר בר חנה, who ruled it impure. Then she brought it to רב יצחק בריה דרב יהודה, who ruled it pure.
steps.simpleTranslation: ילתא brought blood before רבה בר בר חנה, and he ruled her impure. She then brought it before רב יצחק, the son of רב יהודה, and he ruled her pure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story where two sages gave opposite rulings on the same blood. This story sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first sage already ruled 'impure,' and then a second sage ruled 'pure' on the very same case. That looks like the second sage overrode the first, which is what the גמרא will challenge next.

phrases.english: Yalta brought blood
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets, and others have the word in square brackets. Both mean 'she brought.'

phrases.english: before Rabba bar bar Chana,
and he ruled her impure.
She then brought it

phrases.aramaic: לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב יִצְחָק בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: before Rav Yitzchak, son of Rav Yehuda,
and he ruled her pure.

steps.triggerLanguage: יַלְתָּא אַיְיתַאי דְּמָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חַנָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story about examining blood. This time the ruling of one sage is reversed by another.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One sage ruled ילתא's blood impure, and a second sage then ruled it pure.

steps.title: How could the second sage rule pure after the first ruled impure?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב יצחק's ruling using a ברייתא: once a חכם rules something impure or forbidden, another חכם may not rule it pure or permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: How could he do this? Doesn't a ברייתא teach: if a חכם ruled something impure, another חכם may not rule it pure; if he forbade something, another חכם may not permit it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the story it just told. It quotes a ברייתא that seems to forbid exactly what רב יצחק did.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא sets a rule of respect between sages: one sage may not undo the strict ruling of another. רבה בר בר חנה had already ruled 'impure,' so רב יצחק should not have ruled 'pure.' The next step answers this.

keyTerms.meaning: How could he act like this? An opening that challenges something a sage did
A sage who ruled something impure

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule, that one חכם may not overturn another's strict ruling, is an important principle in how halachic rulings work.

phrases.english: But how could he do this?
phrases.notes: 'He' is רב יצחק, the second sage who ruled pure.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: חָכָם שֶׁטִּימֵּא — אֵין חֲבֵרוֹ רַשַּׁאי לְטַהֵר,
phrases.english: A sage who ruled impure — his colleague may not rule pure;
if he forbade — his colleague may not permit!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the action of רב יצחק in the story of step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יצחק בריה דרב יהודה's ruling of 'pure' after רבה בר בר חנה had ruled 'impure.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says one חכם may not rule pure or permitted once another חכם has ruled impure or forbidden. רב יצחק seems to have done exactly that.

steps.title: Why רב יצחק was allowed to rule her pure
steps.stepSummary: רב יצחק first ruled the blood impure. He changed his ruling only after ילתא told him that רבה בר בר חנה always ruled this color pure and was only off now because of his eye pain.
steps.simpleTranslation: At first he ruled her impure. But once she told him, 'Every day he rules this kind of blood pure for me, and only now his eye is hurting him,' he ruled her pure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 15. רב יצחק was not overturning another חכם's real ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא forbids a second חכם from overturning the first חכם's decision. Here רב יצחק first respected the impure ruling. He only changed it once he learned that רבה בר בר חנה's normal ruling on this color was pure, and that this time he simply could not see well. So רב יצחק was not arguing with רבה בר בר חנה's opinion; he was fixing a one-time mistake caused by poor eyesight.

keyTerms.meaning: He was ruling impure (the doubled verb adds emphasis)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רב יצחק ignored the rule against overturning a חכם. He only changed the ruling because the first ruling came from a temporary eye problem, not from a real halachic decision.

phrases.english: At first he was ruling her impure,
phrases.notes: This is רב יצחק בריה דרב יהודה. At first he went along with the impure ruling.

phrases.english: once she said to him
that every day he would rule me pure
with this kind of blood,
and it is only now that he feels pain in his eye,
phrases.notes: She means רבה בר בר חנה. His sore eye made him misjudge the color.

phrases.english: he ruled her pure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge raised in step 15
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: the first ruling was a mistake caused by eyesight, not a real halachic decision
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב יצחק overturned רבה בר בר חנה's ruling, which goes against the ברייתא
steps.terutzMaskana: He first respected the ruling and changed it only once he learned it came from a temporary eye problem

steps.title: Is ילתא believed about this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a woman can be trusted when she claims that a חכם usually rules such blood pure.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is she believed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the answer it just gave. The whole answer depends on ילתא's claim, so can we rely on her word?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 16 rests completely on what ילתא said about רבה בר בר חנה's usual rulings. If a woman is not believed about such things, then רב יצחק had no right to rely on her.

phrases.english: But is she believed?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the reliability of the claim the previous answer depended on
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a woman is believed about claims concerning her blood

steps.title: Yes — a woman is believed about her blood
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers yes and brings a ברייתא: a woman is believed to say 'I saw blood like this and lost it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. And it was taught in a ברייתא: a woman is believed to say, 'I saw blood like this, and I lost it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that she is believed, and supports this with a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא trusts a woman to point to a color and say her lost blood looked like this. That shows the חכמים trust a woman's report about her blood. So ילתא's claim about the color רבה בר בר חנה usually ruled pure can also be trusted.

phrases.english: Yes,
and it was taught in a ברייתא:
A woman is believed to say
"I saw blood like this, and I lost it."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17 with a ברייתא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes, a woman is believed, as the ברייתא of 'I saw like this and lost it' shows
steps.whatToRemember: רב יצחק could rule ילתא pure because רבה בר בר חנה's impure ruling came from his eye pain, and a woman is believed about reports on her blood.

steps.title: Is she believed that a חכם ruled this color pure?
steps.stepSummary: A new question: if a woman says 'blood like this, so-and-so the חכם ruled pure,' is she believed?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: if she says, 'Blood like this, so-and-so the חכם ruled pure,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question that grows out of the ילתא story. Is a woman believed when she reports a חכם's ruling on a color?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is different from the ברייתא. There she reports what she saw, but here she reports what a חכם decided. Here the blood may also still be available to show someone. The question is whether her word about a ruling is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised before them (the חכמים)

phrases.english: A question was asked before them:
"Blood like this, so-and-so the חכם ruled pure,"
what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a related question building on the woman's credibility
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a woman is believed in reporting that a חכם ruled a certain color pure

steps.title: Trying to prove she is believed from the same ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to answer from the ברייתא that a woman is believed to say 'I saw like this and lost it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a woman is believed to say, 'I saw blood like this, and I lost it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the new question using the ברייתא it quoted before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that if a woman is trusted to describe her own blood's color, she should also be trusted to report a חכם's ruling about a color. Either way, the חכמים rely on her word about her blood.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A woman is believed to say
"I saw blood like this, and I lost it,"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attempts to answer the question of step 19
steps.raayaObject: That a woman is believed to report a חכם's ruling on a color
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא: נאמנת אשה לומר כזה ראיתי ואבדתיו

steps.title: No proof — there the blood is gone
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. In the ברייתא the blood is lost, so the חכמים had to rely on her. In our case the blood is still there and can be shown to a חכם.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because the blood is not in front of her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back the proof from step 20. The two cases are not the same.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא the blood was lost, so the only way to rule is to trust her description. In the new question the blood still exists, so it can be brought to a חכם instead of relying on her report. So the ברייתא's leniency does not prove she is believed here, and step 22 tries a different proof.

phrases.english: It is different there,
because it is not in front of her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 20
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof; the question itself is not yet decided
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא is a case where the blood is lost, so the חכמים had no choice but to rely on her; this does not carry over to a case where the blood can still be examined
steps.whatToRemember: Trusting a woman when the blood is lost does not prove we trust her report of a חכם's ruling when the blood can still be shown to a חכם.

steps.title: A proof from the story of יַלְתָּא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the יַלְתָּא story. She showed blood to רבה בר בר חנה, who ruled it impure, and then to רב יצחק בריה דרב יהודה, who first ruled it impure. After she told him רבה בר בר חנה usually rules this kind pure, he ruled it pure. So it seems a woman's claim is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: יַלְתָּא brought blood to רבה בר בר חנה and he ruled it impure. She brought it to רב יצחק son of רב יהודה and he ruled it pure. We asked: how could he do that? A ברייתא teaches that once one חכם rules impure, another may not rule pure! And we answered: at first he also ruled it impure. But she told him that every day רבה בר בר חנה rules this kind pure, and only today his eye hurts. So he changed and ruled it pure. This shows she is believed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is trying to answer the open question from step 19 by quoting an earlier story. In that story, a חכם changed his ruling after a woman told him what another חכם usually does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was whether we believe a woman who says 'a חכם ruled blood like this pure.' In the story, רב יצחק first ruled impure, and then switched to pure right after יַלְתָּא's claim. So it looks like her word is what changed the outcome, which would prove she is believed.

keyTerms.term: חָכָם שֶׁטִּימֵּא אֵין חֲבֵירוֹ רַשַּׁאי לְטַהֵר
keyTerms.meaning: Once one חכם rules impure, a second חכם may not rule the same thing pure

steps.confusionAlert: There are two rabbis here. רבה בר בר חנה is the one who usually rules pure but had eye pain this time. רב יצחק בריה דרב יהודה is the second rabbi, who changed his ruling.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
That Yalta brought blood
phrases.notes: Some versions read אייתא and some read אייתאי. Both mean 'she brought.'

phrases.english: before Rabba bar bar Ḥana
and he ruled her impure.

phrases.aramaic: לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב יִצְחָק בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה
phrases.english: She then brought it before Rav Yitzḥak son of Rav Yehuda
and he ruled her pure.
And how could he do this?
But isn't it taught: 'A sage who ruled something impure,
his colleague may not rule it pure,' etc.?
And we said: he really was ruling her impure,
phrases.notes: 'He' here is רב יצחק. At first he also ruled it impure.

phrases.english: but once she told him

phrases.aramaic: דְּכֹל יוֹמָא מְדַכֵּי לַהּ כִּי הַאי גַוְנָא,
phrases.english: that every day he rules her pure with this kind,
phrases.notes: 'He' here is רבה בר בר חנה, the first rabbi.

phrases.english: and it is only now that his eye hurts
he went back and ruled her pure.
Evidently, she is believed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was rejected in step 21, the גמרא offers a second proof for the question of step 19.
steps.raayaObject: That a woman is believed when she says a חכם rules blood like this pure.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of יַלְתָּא with רבה בר בר חנה and רב יצחק בריה דרב יהודה, where he changed to pure after hearing her claim.

steps.title: He relied on his own learning
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. רב יצחק did not rule pure because he trusted יַלְתָּא. He already knew from his own learning that this blood was pure.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יצחק בר יהודה relied on what he had learned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from the יַלְתָּא story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יצחק knew from his own learning that this color is pure. He held back only out of respect for רבה בר בר חנה, who had ruled impure. Her words removed that worry, but his actual ruling came from his own knowledge, so the story shows nothing about believing her.
steps.whatToRemember: The יַלְתָּא story cannot prove that a woman is believed about what a חכם ruled. The ruling there rested on the second חכם's own knowledge, not on her claim.

phrases.aramaic: רַב יִצְחָק בַּר יְהוּדָה אַגְּמָרֵיהּ סְמַךְ.
phrases.english: Rav Yitzḥak bar Yehuda relied on his own learning.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יִצְחָק בַּר יְהוּדָה אַגְּמָרֵיהּ סְמַךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 22.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the story. The question from step 19 stays open.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed he ruled pure because of her claim. In fact he ruled from his own knowledge.

steps.title: רבי rules on the same blood three times
steps.stepSummary: A new story: רבי saw blood at night and ruled it impure. By day he ruled it pure. After an hour he went back to impure, and then worried that he had made a mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי saw blood at night and ruled it impure. He saw it by day and ruled it pure. He waited an hour and ruled it impure again. He said: Woe is me, perhaps I made a mistake!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story about how hard it can be to judge the color of blood. It shows רבי changing his ruling on the same stain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same blood looked different at night and in daylight, so רבי's ruling changed. He finally went back to his first ruling of impure. Even then he worried that he had made a mistake. The story shows how unsure even a great חכם can be when judging colors.

keyTerms.meaning: He went back (changed his ruling again)

phrases.english: Rebbi saw blood at night and ruled it impure;
he saw it by day and ruled it pure;
he waited one hour and went back and ruled it impure.
He said: Woe is me, perhaps I made a mistake!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the question about believing the woman to a new story about רבי ruling on one stain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ruled on the same blood as impure, then pure, then impure again, and worried that he had erred.

steps.title: Did רבי really make a mistake?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions רבי's worry. If he went back to impure because of how the blood looked before, he certainly erred, since a ברייתא forbids a חכם to rule 'if it were moist it would be impure.'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Perhaps I erred?' He definitely erred! A ברייתא teaches: a חכם may not say, 'If this blood were still moist, it would certainly be impure.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the way the story was told. It says רבי did not just 'maybe' make a mistake. If the story happened as told, he certainly made one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ברייתא teaches that a חכם must judge the blood as it looks now, not guess how it looked earlier when it was wet. Going back to 'impure' because the blood once looked darker would be exactly that forbidden guess. So the story as first told cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: If it had been (judging by an earlier state instead of what is seen now)

phrases.english: Perhaps I erred?
phrases.notes: The גמרא is quoting רבי's worry from the end of the story in step 24.

phrases.english: He certainly erred!
As it is taught: a Sage may not say:
"If it were moist,
it would certainly have been impure."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ending of רבי's story told in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's final ruling of impure and his worry that he erred.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא forbids ruling based on how the blood looked when wet. Going back to impure because of the earlier look would be a clear mistake, not a possible one.

steps.title: A judge rules only by what he sees
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא retells the story: רבי ruled each time by what his eyes saw. At night it looked impure. In the morning it looked different, so he thought the night light misled him. When it changed again, he understood it was impure blood slowly fading.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he said: A judge can only go by what his eyes see. At first he held it as impure. When he saw in the morning that it had changed, he said: it was surely pure all along, and only at night it could not be seen well. When he saw it changed again, he said: this is impure, and it is just fading more and more.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by telling the story a different way. רבי never said 'perhaps I erred.' He explained each ruling by what he actually saw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each ruling was based on the blood's look at that moment, so רבי never broke the rule 'do not judge by how it looked when wet.' The second change showed him that the color keeps fading over time. So he understood that the blood was really impure and was just getting lighter.

keyTerms.term: אֵין לוֹ לַדַּיָּין אֶלָּא מַה שֶּׁעֵינָיו רוֹאוֹת
keyTerms.meaning: A judge has only what his eyes see
He held it as, treated it as

steps.whatToRemember: A חכם judges blood only by how it looks in front of him now. He does not guess how it looked before.

phrases.english: Rather, (he said):
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets, and some leave it out.

phrases.english: A judge has nothing
except what his eyes see.
At first he held it as impure.
Once he saw in the morning that it had changed,
he said: It was surely pure,
and it was only at night that it could not be seen well.
Once he saw that it changed again, he said:
This is impure,
and it is fading, getting lighter as it goes.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אֵין לוֹ לַדַּיָּין אֶלָּא מַה שֶּׁעֵינָיו רוֹאוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 25 by retelling the story.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי went back to impure because of how the blood looked earlier, and so he worried he had erred.
steps.terutzMaskana: Every ruling followed what he saw at that moment. The fading showed that the blood was really impure.

steps.title: How different חכמים checked blood
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reports that רבי checked blood by candlelight, and רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסף checked it on a cloudy day between the pillars.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי would check blood by the light of a candle. רבי ישמעאל son of רבי יוסף would check blood on a cloudy day, between the pillars.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new related topic: in what kind of light the חכמים checked blood colors. It reports the practice of two great חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both practices show checking in weak light: candlelight, or a dim spot on a cloudy day. These were great experts, so they could check even in poor light. The next lines give the general rule for proper lighting.

phrases.english: Rabbi would check by candlelight.
Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosef would check
on a cloudy day, between the pillars.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the story about lighting (night against day) to how חכמים actually checked blood.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי checked by candlelight, and רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסף checked between pillars on a cloudy day.

steps.title: Check blood between sun and shade
steps.stepSummary: רב אמי בר שמואל rules that in all cases, blood is checked only in a spot between sunlight and shade.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אמי בר שמואל said: In all these cases, we check blood only between the sun and the shade.
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא gives a general rule for proper lighting when checking blood. The best place is between direct sun and shade.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Too much light or too little light can make a color look wrong. A spot between sun and shade gives the clearest view of the true color.

keyTerms.meaning: And all of them, in every case

phrases.english: Rav Ami bar Shmuel said:
And all of them, we do not check them
except between the sun and the shade.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכוּלָּן אֵין בּוֹדְקִין אוֹתָן אֶלָּא בֵּין חַמָּה לְצֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the general lighting rule after the examples in step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Blood is checked only between sunlight and shade.

steps.title: In the sun, under the shade of one's hand
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן in the name of רבה בר אבוה gives a different practical method: stand in the sun and look at the blood under the shade of your hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: One checks in the sun, under the shade of his hand.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives his own way to get the right light. You stand in the sunlight and shade the blood with your hand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This also mixes sun and shade, but in a simple, hands-on way. The light around is strong, but the blood itself is shaded, so the color shows clearly.

phrases.aramaic: רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: Rav Nachman said in the name of Rabba bar Avuh:
In the sun, and in the shade of his hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ בְּחַמָּה וּבְצֵל יָדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another way of lighting the blood, next to רב אמי בר שמואל's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Check the blood while standing in the sun, with the blood under the shade of one's hand.
steps.whatToRemember: Proper lighting matters for checking blood. Use a mix of sun and shade, or stand in the sun and shade the blood with your hand.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: the color of diluted wine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's color 'like diluted wine, two parts' and opens a ברייתא that will explain it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And like diluted wine, two parts, etc.' A ברייתא taught:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the next phrase of the משנה, about a color like diluted wine. It is setting up a ברייתא that comes right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists impure colors, and one of them is like wine mixed with two parts water. 'תנא' opens a ברייתא, and its words continue on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: Like diluted wine (wine mixed with water)

phrases.english: "And like diluted wine, two parts," etc.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from our משנה. The full line is two parts water with one part wine from the שרון.

phrases.english: It was taught:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of lighting and goes back to the next color listed in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Quotes the משנה's diluted-wine color and opens a ברייתא that explains it.
